principle.name: System Thinking Over Component Thinking
principle.description: Always evaluate the system as a whole rather than individual components in isolation. Consider the full lifecycle, data flows, and integration points when making architectural decisions.
principle.rationale: Architecture decisions have ripple effects across the entire system. Component-level optimization can lead to system-level problems.

example.good: Consider how caching affects data consistency, user experience, and system performance across all services
example.bad: Optimizing cache for a single service without considering system-wide data flow implications

principle.name: Principle of Least Astonishment
principle.description: Prefer the simplest architecture that meets requirements. Avoid over-engineering and unnecessary complexity.
principle.rationale: Simple architectures are easier to understand, maintain, and evolve. Complex solutions often introduce more failure points and technical debt.

example.good: Start with a simple monolith if the business requirements don't justify microservices complexity
example.bad: Implementing microservices because they're trendy without clear business need

principle.name: Evolutionary Architecture
principle.description: Design systems that can evolve and adapt over time. Avoid architectural decisions that lock the system into a specific technology or approach.
principle.rationale: Business requirements and technology landscapes change. Systems must be able to adapt without complete rewrites.

example.good: Choose database technology that allows for easy migration and supports multiple vendors if needed
example.bad: Locking into a proprietary database that limits future options

principle.name: Domain-Driven Design
principle.description: Align architecture with business domains and bounded contexts. Use clear boundaries between different business domains.
principle.rationale: DDD helps manage complexity, improves communication between business and technical teams, and creates more maintainable systems.

example.good: Define clear interfaces between bounded contexts based on business capabilities
example.bad: Allowing arbitrary calls between any services without clear domain boundaries

principle.name: Security by Design
principle.description: Build security into the architecture from the beginning rather than bolting it on later.
principle.rationale: Security considerations should influence architectural decisions, not be an afterthought.

example.good: Design authentication as part of the core architecture with proper threat modeling
example.bad: Adding authentication as an overlay without considering system-wide security implications

principle.name: Performance-First Architecture
principle.description: Consider performance implications from the start of design. Make architectural decisions that support performance requirements.
principle.rationale: Performance is often harder to add later than to design for initially.

example.good: Design data flows to minimize latency and maximize throughput
example.bad: Creating chatty architectures with excessive round-trips

principle.name: Documentation-Driven Architecture
principle.description: Document architectural decisions and their rationale. Use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture important decisions.
principle.rationale: Documentation ensures continuity, helps new team members understand decisions, and provides audit trail for architectural choices.

category.name: system_thinking
category.item: Evaluated system as whole, not just components
Considered full lifecycle and data flows

pattern.name: layered_architecture
pattern.benefits: Clear separation of responsibilities, easier testing, independent evolution
pattern.considerations: Ensure clear interfaces between layers, avoid circular dependencies

example.good: Presentation → Business Logic → Data Access → Database
example.bad: Mixing UI logic with business logic

pattern.name: microservices_architecture
pattern.description: Decompose system into small, independent services
pattern.benefits: Independent deployment, technology diversity, team autonomy, fault isolation
pattern.considerations: Service boundaries must be clear, communication overhead managed, data consistency addressed

example.good: Order Service, User Service, Payment Service, Inventory Service

pattern.name: event_driven_architecture
pattern.description: Use events to decouple components and enable asynchronous communication
pattern.benefits: Loose coupling, better scalability, event sourcing, easier debugging
pattern.considerations: Event schema design, idempotency, error handling, monitoring requirements

pattern.name: cqrs_architecture
pattern.description: Command Query Responsibility Segregation for read/write separation
pattern.benefits: Optimized for different query patterns, clear separation of concerns, better performance
pattern.considerations: Define command and query responsibilities, ensure eventual consistency

example.bad: Mixed read/write operations in single service

pattern.name: hexagonal_architecture
pattern.description: Six-sided architecture with ports and adapters
pattern.considerations: Port definitions must be stable, adapters handle complexity, avoid breaking changes

example.good: Core system with well-defined plugin interfaces, versioned adapters
example.bad: Direct plugin modifications without interface versioning

criteria.name: scalability
criteria.description: Assess horizontal and vertical scaling capabilities

criteria.name: security
criteria.description: Evaluate security posture and threat resistance

criteria.name: maintainability
criteria.description: Assess long-term maintenance and evolution capabilities

guideline.name: stakeholder_communication
guideline.description: Communicate architectural decisions effectively to all stakeholders

practices.practice: Use Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) for important decisions
Provide clear rationale with trade-off analysis
Keep documentation updated with system changes
